strengths: The manuscript presents a clear, relevant idea: learn a small task-triggering mask and prune selected KV-cache dimensions to mitigate indirect prompt injection without altering the prompt or requiring additional inference-time LLM calls. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/5b472df5ef904090a3ce1ab8dc413495/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The reported reductions in attack success rate are substantial across two open-weight models and three task settings, while clean-task quality is generally retained.

Ablations over pruning rate, masking strength, and attributed response length help characterize the proposed mechanism. The text-to-code transfer experiment provides some initial evidence that a learned mask can generalize beyond one injection form.
The method could complement prompt-formatting defenses, and its low per-query overhead is practically attractive when contexts or masks can be reused.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification is not valid as written. Conditions (19)–(20) do not imply S>0; the DPO sign/minimization convention and claimed KL relation are confused; Jensen's inequality yields a bound involving log σ(βE[S]), not the quantity defined as the upper bound in (24); and the transition in (28) replaces the dataset response distribution with model probabilities without justification. Consequently, Theorem 1 does not establish the claimed DPO upper bound, while Lemma 1 only describes extreme limits and does not justify the practical surrogate or its sample efficiency.

The evaluation is insufficient for a security claim. It uses only two 7–8B models, mostly one processed QA benchmark, a constructed WildChat condition, and relatively weak prompt-formatting baselines. There are no adaptive attacks, held-out attack families of meaningful breadth, agent/tool-use scenarios, stronger defenses evaluated on an accuracy–cost tradeoff, or analysis of false positives on benign instruction-like context.

The learned defense appears model- and task-specific and requires eight labeled examples containing known injections plus constructed clean and poisoned responses. Masks are learned separately for each dataset, but the paper does not adequately discuss this supervision, deployment assumption, or whether test attacks share templates or generation procedures with the attribution pool. The limited code/text transfer study does not establish open-world generalization.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the exact model checkpoints and chat templates, test-set sizes, attack instructions and placement procedure, ASR labeling method, GPT judge model and prompt, decoding settings, seeds, hardware, implementation details for modifying KV caches, and aggregation across attribution examples are missing. No code or artifact availability statement is provided.

The mechanistic interpretation is overstated. Gradient-times-activation identifies locally influential dimensions, but pruning them does not show that they encode a general data-versus-instruction distinction. Missing controls include random or magnitude-matched pruning, ablation of the subset Φ, comparisons with alternative attribution methods, mask stability across samples, and tests for effects on unrelated capabilities.

Claims of statistical significance are unsupported: results average only three trials, uncertainty sources are unclear, test sample counts are absent, and no significance tests or confidence intervals over evaluation examples are reported. Several analyses also contain labeling or exposition errors, such as referring to Figure 5 where Figure 4 is intended.

The empirical idea may be recoverable, but correcting the theory, fully specifying the method, and substantially broadening the adversarial and reproducibility evaluation are necessary before the work meets the soundness standard for Findings. These revisions appear feasible for a future cycle, motivating an OA of 2 rather than rejection without resubmission.

strengths: The paper targets an important, clearly NLP-relevant security problem and proposes an appealing intervention: modifying only context-token KV-cache dimensions, without retraining the underlying model or altering the visible prompt.

The empirical section evaluates both attack success and task quality on two models and three tasks. It also includes useful ablations over pruning rate, response-prefix length, mask strength, and cross-attack transfer.

The reported results are promising: CachePrune often substantially reduces attack success while approximately preserving clean-task performance, unlike Base64 encoding, which seriously damages utility.

The paper is generally easy to follow, and its diagrams and tables communicate the intended workflow clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/6e184286f43a40ada5447cf0f5c46517/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation contains major errors. The paper calls E[S] an upper bound on the stated DPO objective, but Jensen's inequality only yields LDPO <= log sigma(beta E[S]); E[S] itself is not the claimed numerical upper bound. The defined objective also reverses the usual preferred/rejected DPO orientation and is discussed inconsistently as something to minimize. Moreover, assumptions (19)-(20) do not imply S>0, and Equation (28) replaces the empirical response distribution with model probabilities without justification. Consequently, Theorem 1 does not establish the claimed DPO basis for the attribution loss.

The pruning rule is not mathematically well-defined as written. In Equation (5), the supremum over thresholds whose upper-tail probability is at most p is positive infinity, because all sufficiently large thresholds satisfy the condition; it would therefore prune nothing. Equation (13) additionally normalizes signed gradient-times-activation scores by their sums, which can be zero or negative, but no stabilization or sign convention is specified. These are central algorithmic details rather than cosmetic notation issues.

The clean and poisoned targets used for attribution are obtained from different, manually modified prompts: the injection is removed to produce one target, while an extra trigger instruction is added to produce the other. Thus the resulting gradients may identify artifacts of these prompt modifications or task content rather than general 'data-versus-instruction neurons.' Eight attribution examples are insufficient to establish that the masks are stable, general, or mechanistically meaningful.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits the number of test examples, exact prompts and templates, ASR labeling procedure, generation settings, injected-instruction inventory, GPT-judge model and prompt, statistical-testing details, and implementation-level masking procedure. Reporting variation over three masks does not replace confidence intervals over test examples or significance tests.

The security evaluation is too narrow for the central defense claim. It covers two small open models, mostly one benchmark-derived injection setup, and simple formatting baselines. It does not evaluate diverse or adaptive attacks, unseen instruction families, longer contexts, multilingual inputs, agent/tool-use settings, or current stronger defenses. Table 4 provides only limited code/text transfer and still uses SQuAD.

The claimed efficiency is not demonstrated. Attribution requires backward computations, yet no attribution cost, memory overhead, latency, cache-storage overhead, or comparison under a matched compute budget is reported. Saying that the method introduces no test-time computation is also too strong because cache masking itself is an operation, even if potentially inexpensive.

Several interpretations go beyond the evidence. Lower ASR after masking does not establish that particular neurons encode the model's own distinction between data and instructions, and the middle-layer distribution is not a causal validation. Likewise, experiments on a small set of synthetic-style attacks do not support the broad claim that context is thereafter treated 'exclusively as pure data.'

Overall, the idea and preliminary results are interesting, but the invalid core derivation, ill-specified pruning equation, and incomplete evaluation prevent a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation. Correcting the method specification and rebuilding the evaluation could plausibly produce a next-cycle resubmission, so a score of 2 is more appropriate than rejection without resubmission.

strengths: CachePrune offers an interesting, relevant defense: it suppresses attribution-selected KV-cache dimensions only over the untrusted context span, requiring neither model retraining nor additional generation calls for each protected request.

The main results are promising across two open-weight model families and three tasks. CachePrune usually reduces attack success substantially while preserving or improving clean-task performance, unlike Base64 encoding, which severely damages utility.

The paper includes useful initial analyses of pruning rate, mask strength, response-prefix length, layer distribution, and transfer between text- and code-derived attacks. Results over three attribution-sample draws provide some indication of stability.

The paper is generally organized around a clear motivation, and using only eight attribution examples to construct a reusable mask could make the method practically attractive if validated more rigorously.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the central attribution loss is not sound as written. The proof substitutes model probabilities for the unspecified data distribution in the DPO expectation (Eq. 28), so the entropy decomposition does not follow without an additional, strong definition of the preference-data distribution. The reference-model conditions in Eqs. 19–20 also do not imply S>0; Eq. 20 even compares the poisoned reference probability with the clean model probability. Moreover, Jensen bounds the stated DPO quantity by log-sigmoid of an expectation, but the paper then declares that expectation itself to be the upper-bound objective. The claim that minimizing the DPO objective minimizes KL to the reference model is also unjustified. These are central derivational problems rather than typographical details.

The proposed loss remains heuristic even if the faulty DPO derivation is removed. The endpoint limits in Lemma 1 do not establish useful correspondence away from extreme probabilities, and no experiment compares this loss against simpler contrastive log-probability or gradient-attribution alternatives. Thus the claimed sample-efficiency benefit of the derived objective is not isolated.

The empirical protocol is insufficiently specified for reproducibility. The paper omits test-set sizes, exact prompts and injection templates, the operational rule or annotator used to label attack success, the identity and prompt of the WildChat LLM judge, decoding details beyond greediness, model checkpoints/configurations, hardware, and implementation/code availability. It is also unclear whether masks are separately fitted for every dataset and attack setting and what randomness the three trials cover.

Evaluation breadth is too limited for a security claim: only two 7–8B models are tested, apparently on benchmark-style or manually strengthened injections. There is no adaptive attacker who knows the defense, no established multi-attack benchmark or agent/tool-use setting, and no analysis of false positives on benign imperative text embedded in context. Consequently, the claim that pruning enforces treatment of context as pure data is substantially stronger than the evidence.

The comparison excludes training-based and extra-compute defenses instead of reporting their security–quality–cost trade-offs. Restricting the table to several relatively weak prompt transformations makes it difficult to assess competitiveness with stronger contemporary defenses. The claim of significant improvement is also unsupported by hypothesis tests or uncertainty for the baselines.

Several mechanistic conclusions are overinterpreted. Concentration of selected dimensions in middle layers does not establish that they encode an abstract data-versus-instruction distinction, and differences between selected key and value dimensions do not show how a model was trained to perceive instructions. Causal controls such as random pruning, magnitude-matched pruning, shuffled masks, and clean-task-specific pruning are missing.

Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but the invalid central derivation and incomplete security/reproducibility evaluation prevent a Findings recommendation. Correcting or reframing the theory, fully specifying the protocol, and adding strong controls and adaptive evaluations appear feasible for a substantially revised next-cycle submission.

strengths: The paper proposes a technically interesting intervention: a small, model-specific mask learned by gradient-based attribution is applied directly to context KV-cache dimensions, avoiding prompt rewriting and additional LLM calls once the mask has been learned.

Across three open-weight model families, SQuAD, HotpotQA, and dialogue summarization, CachePrune generally reduces attack success substantially while preserving clean-task utility better than the evaluated prompt-formatting defenses.

The evaluation includes useful ablations over pruning ratio, attribution sample count, response-prefix length, masking strength, and selective thresholding. Transfer experiments across injection types and an initial adaptive-attack study add evidence beyond a single static attack.

The distinction between clean-task quality, attacked-task quality, and attack success is valuable: it prevents a low attack-success rate caused simply by destroying the model's ability to use the context from being presented as a successful defense.
weaknesses: The mathematical justification is not sound as written. In the proof of Theorem 1, the conditions imposed on the reference model do not imply the claimed sign of the log-ratio difference; the expectation under the fixed preference dataset is then replaced by expectations weighted by the evaluated model without justification; and Jensen's inequality only bounds the transformed log-sigmoid expression, not the newly defined linear quantity in the stated sense. Consequently, the claimed DPO upper bound and its connection to the attribution loss are not established.

The empirical scope is too narrow for the broad security claims. The main experiments use templated injections inserted into QA contexts and a constructed dialogue condition, rather than realistic document, retrieval, tool-use, or agent attacks. Transfer is tested among only a small family of related instructions, so the evidence does not establish that the learned mask generally separates data from instructions.

Comparisons omit strong relevant defenses, including activation/task-drift methods cited by the paper and training-based structured-query defenses. Dismissing these as computationally unfair is insufficient without an accuracy-cost comparison. No latency, memory, mask-learning cost, or implementation-overhead measurements support the claims of efficiency and scalability, and complementarity with other defenses is asserted but not tested.

The adaptive evaluation is not yet a convincing worst-case test. It optimizes the paper's first-token proxy for only a limited number of GCG iterations, is acknowledged to become trapped in poor local optima on two models, and does not directly optimize attack success or test stronger target-sequence, transfer, or black-box attacks. Robustness and security-critical applicability are therefore overstated.

The mechanistic interpretation is stronger than the evidence. KV-cache coordinates are repeatedly called 'neurons,' while gradient-times-activation scores and pruning effects do not demonstrate that these dimensions encode a causal, general notion of data versus instruction. The layer- and key/value-level interpretations are especially speculative. Moreover, the normalization in Eq. 10 divides signed attribution scores by their signed sum, which may be near zero or negative; stability safeguards and sensitivity analyses are not provided.

Important reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous: exact test-set sizes, random seeds, complete prompts/templates and baseline settings, precise model checkpoints, decoding parameters, hyperparameter-selection procedure, and a runnable implementation. The closed, versioned GPT judge further limits reproducibility, and its displayed rubric orders 1 as best and 5 as worst while the reported metric marks larger values as better without explaining the conversion.

The presentation contains numerous grammatical and notation errors, including inconsistent index ranges and several mistakes in the proofs. Statistical uncertainty is reported only for CachePrune, with no significance testing or comparable variation for baselines. These issues make both the method and its claimed gains harder to audit.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP security problem and proposes a practically interesting defense: a reusable mask over context KV-cache dimensions, requiring neither prompt reformatting nor additional LLM calls for each query.

The reported improvements are substantial across three open-weight model families, two QA datasets, and a dialogue-summarization setting. The paper also includes pruning-ratio, sample-count, loss-length, selective-thresholding, transfer, and adaptive-attack studies.

The distinction between clean-task quality, attacked-task quality, and attack success rate is useful, and the results suggest that the method can outperform the tested prompt-engineering defenses without the severe utility loss of Base64 encoding.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is not valid as written. Equation 7 places the poisoned response in the preferred position of the stated DPO expression, yet the surrounding discussion treats minimization of that expression as favoring the clean response. In the proof, assumptions (20)-(21) do not imply S>0, and equation (21) itself appears to compare the reference probability of a poisoned response with the model probability of a clean response. The subsequent Jensen argument, response-distribution decomposition, and claimed upper bound therefore do not establish the advertised connection between the attribution loss and DPO.

The attribution construction is heuristic and insufficiently validated. Clean and poisoned targets are generated under modified prompts—by removing the injection or adding “Answer this at the end”—and then approximated using only their first token. The paper does not establish that gradients for these counterfactual first tokens identify a general data-versus-instruction mechanism rather than attack-template or lexical artifacts.

The mechanistic claims are overstated. Gradient-times-activation scores and successful masking do not demonstrate that the selected KV dimensions are “task-triggering neurons” or encode the model's intrinsic distinction between data and instructions. No causal controls, random or magnitude-matched masking baselines, attribution-method comparisons, or stability/overlap analyses are provided. The signed normalization in Equation 10 can also be unstable when attribution scores cancel or their sum approaches zero.

The empirical comparison is too narrow for a security claim. The baselines are primarily simple prompt transformations, while stronger training-based, activation-based, detection, and multi-call defenses are excluded as “unfair.” Different cost profiles do not make comparison inappropriate; effectiveness-versus-compute and utility trade-offs should be measured explicitly.

Generalization is limited. Masks are learned from injected examples, evaluation assumes a known context boundary and fixed templates, and transfer is examined mostly within SQuAD over a small collection of related attack instructions. There is no evaluation on tool-using agents, retrieved web content, long or heterogeneous contexts, multilingual inputs, unseen prompt templates, or stronger adaptive attacks designed to evade the learned mask.

The adaptive evaluation does not justify the claim of immunity. The GCG attack succeeds strongly only on LLaMA3, is weak even against undefended Mistral and Phi models, and the paper itself acknowledges optimization difficulty. This leaves unclear whether CachePrune is robust or whether the attack failed to find effective sequences.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting are inadequate. No code or artifact link is supplied; test-set sizes, exact prompt templates for the main QA experiments, generation settings, operational ASR labeling procedure, model revisions, hardware/runtime, and mask-learning cost are incompletely reported. Error bars cover only CachePrune, with three mask trials, while baseline uncertainty and significance tests are absent.

The claim of negligible test-time overhead is not quantified. Cache editing still requires implementation-specific operations, while mask construction requires gradient computation and labeled clean/poisoned counterfactuals. Memory, latency, attribution cost, cache-reuse assumptions, and compatibility with optimized serving systems are not measured.

Overall, the empirical signal is promising enough to motivate resubmission, but the incorrect theory, weak causal evidence, incomplete security evaluation, and insufficient reproducibility prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current form. The paper should correct or remove the DPO analysis, narrow its mechanistic claims, add rigorous controls and stronger baselines, and provide a reproducible evaluation on genuinely unseen attacks and deployment settings.

strengths: The paper presents a creative and highly relevant defense: identifying attribution-selected KV-cache dimensions and masking them only over the context span. This avoids model retraining, prompt reformatting, and additional per-query LLM calls.

The empirical gains are substantial across three open-weight model families. CachePrune generally reduces attack success rates considerably while retaining clean-answer quality; for example, on SQuAD it lowers LLaMA3-8B ASR from 27.86 to 7.44 and Mistral-7B ASR from 9.01 to 0.68.

The evaluation is broader than a single benchmark: it includes SQuAD, HotpotQA, and dialogue summarization, plus code/text attacks, transfer between attack instructions, a GCG-based adaptive attack, and several response-quality metrics.

Useful ablations examine the number of attribution samples, pruning rate, response-prefix length, masking strength, and selective-thresholding constraint. The results support the importance of the proposed design choices, particularly selective thresholding at larger pruning rates.
The method is explained clearly enough to understand its main implementation, and the assumption that context boundaries are known is stated explicitly.
weaknesses: The DPO-based theoretical justification contains serious gaps. In Appendix C, the conditions in Equations 20–21 do not imply the claimed sign of S in Equation 22; the paper uses a nonstandard signed DPO objective without clearly specifying optimization direction; and Equation 29 replaces the preference-data distribution with model probabilities without justification. The asymptotic lemma is consequently weak evidence for the proposed loss. These problems undermine the theoretical narrative, although not necessarily the empirical method.

The baseline comparison is incomplete. The experiments mainly compare against relatively weak prompt-formatting defenses, while stronger fine-tuning, detection/filtering, and multi-call defenses are dismissed as computationally incomparable. Those methods could still be compared on security, utility, and measured cost, or included as reference upper bounds.

Claims that the approach is lightweight and scalable are not backed by latency, memory, preprocessing-time, or attribution-cost measurements. CachePrune also requires white-box KV-cache modification, known context boundaries, and a separately learned mask, which materially limits deployment compared with the broad practical framing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript gives no code link, exact evaluation-set sizes or example identifiers, random seeds, complete generation templates, or sufficiently precise operational details for deciding whether a QA response is poisoned. Referring to a split prepared by prior work is not enough to reconstruct the evaluation reliably.

Generalization remains limited. Masks are learned separately from attack-aware clean/poisoned examples for each model and apparent task setting; cross-dataset or cross-domain mask transfer is not evaluated. The study also excludes larger models, multilingual inputs, long contexts, tool-using agents, and realistic retrieved web content.

The adaptive-attack section lacks important evaluation details, including a clear separation between attack optimization and evaluation examples. Moreover, the implemented GCG attack is highly effective only on LLaMA3-8B, making robustness conclusions for the other models less informative.

The paper sometimes overinterprets behavioral interventions as mechanistic evidence. Successful gradient-based pruning does not by itself establish that the selected dimensions encode the model's intrinsic definition of “data versus instruction”; stronger causal controls and comparisons with random or magnitude-matched masks would be needed.

There are numerous presentation and notation issues, including reversed context indices in the intervention description, inconsistent terminology and equation references, and substantial grammatical errors. Overall, the empirical contribution appears promising and suitable for Findings, but the theoretical errors, incomplete baseline coverage, and missing reproducibility details prevent a main-conference recommendation.
